title: Tags: naming a version you can return to
objective: By the end of this lesson you can mark a release so anyone can reproduce that exact state later, and you know why a tag is treated differently from a branch.

blocks.text: A branch moves. A tag does not. When you ship something, you need a name for exactly what you shipped — so that six weeks later, when a customer reports a problem with version 2.3, you can stand on the exact code they are running rather than approximately that code.

blocks.caption: Creating and pushing a tag
lines: git tag -a v2.3.0 -m "Bulk upload, faster report export"
git push origin v2.3.0        # tags do NOT travel with a normal push
git show v2.3.0                # what it points at, plus the message

rows: A real object: author, date, message

blocks.title: Use annotated tags for anything real
blocks.text: The extra flag records who tagged it, when, and why. That metadata is what makes a release history readable a year later, and it costs you one -a and one -m.
Semantic versioning is the widespread convention: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. It exists so that a version number tells someone whether upgrading is safe.

rows: Fixed a bug, nothing else changed
Added a feature, existing use still works
Changed or removed something people depend on

blocks.title: The point of the major number
blocks.text: It is a promise about compatibility, not a marketing decision. A team that avoids bumping the major number because it 'looks like a big deal' ends up shipping breaking changes inside a patch release — and then nobody can trust any version number they publish.

blocks.caption: Investigating a version
lines: git switch --detach v2.3.0     # stand exactly on what was released
# reproduce the bug, read the code as it was
git switch -                   # come back to your work
git log --oneline v2.3.0..v2.4.0    # what changed between two releases
git diff v2.3.0 v2.4.0 -- src/upload/   # in one area only
git describe --tags                 # how far the current commit is from the last tag

blocks.text: That first command is the reason tags matter operationally. A support question about a specific version becomes a two-command investigation instead of an argument about which commit was probably deployed.
Fixing a released version without shipping everything else

blocks.caption: The patch branch pattern
lines: git switch -c release/2.3 v2.3.0     # a branch starting from the released tag
git cherry-pick a3f91c2              # bring in just the fix commit from main
git tag -a v2.3.1 -m "Fix timezone on report export"

blocks.text: cherry-pick copies one commit's changes onto the branch you are on. This is how a critical fix reaches customers on an older version without dragging along everything else that has landed on main since.

blocks.title: Never move or reuse a published tag
blocks.text: People and build systems record 'we are running v2.3.0' and trust that it means one specific state. Moving that tag makes every one of those records a lie, and machines that already downloaded it will not agree with machines that download it later. If you tagged the wrong commit, publish v2.3.1 instead.

blocks.caption: The commands, including the ones to avoid
lines: git push origin --tags          # push all tags at once
git fetch --tags                # get tags others created
git tag -d v2.3.0-typo          # delete locally (fine, if never pushed)
git push origin --delete v2.3.0-typo   # delete on the server — only for genuine mistakes

blocks.title: Tag a release and investigate it
steps: Run: git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "First working version" && git push origin v0.1.0
Run: echo 'new feature' >> notes.txt && git commit -am "Add a feature"
Run: git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "Add the feature" && git push origin v0.2.0
Run: git tag && git show v0.1.0 | head
Run: git log --oneline v0.1.0..v0.2.0      (what changed between releases)
Run: git switch --detach v0.1.0 && cat notes.txt   (the released state exactly)
blocks.expected: Two annotated tags, the difference between them listed, and the earlier release state standing in front of you. That last step is the whole reason tags exist.

cheatsheet: A branch moves; a tag is a permanent name for one commit
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "..." — always annotated for releases
Tags do not travel with a normal push: git push origin <tag> or --tags
git fetch --tags to receive tags others created
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch = safe fix, minor = safe addition, major = breaking
git switch --detach <tag> stands exactly on a released state
git log v1..v2 — what changed between two releases
git describe --tags — how far you are from the last tag
cherry-pick one fix onto a release branch instead of shipping all of main
Never move a published tag; publish the next patch version instead

checkpoint.prompt: What is the difference between a tag and a branch?

choices.A: A tag stores the files separately
choices.B: There is none; a tag is a read-only branch
choices.C: A tag can only be created by maintainers
choices.D: A branch moves forward as you commit

checkpoint.explanation: A tag is a permanent name for one specific commit. That permanence is the point: a released version needs a name that will still mean the same state in a year.

checkpoint.prompt: You created a tag and pushed your branch, but colleagues cannot see the tag. Why?

choices.A: Only annotated tags are pushed, lightweight ones stay local
choices.D: Tags need git push origin <tag> or --tags to travel

checkpoint.explanation: It is a common surprise. Pushing a branch sends commits, not tags.

checkpoint.prompt: A change removes a function other teams call. Which version bump is correct?

choices.A: PATCH — it is only one function
choices.B: MINOR — something was removed, not added
choices.C: No bump; document it in the notes
choices.D: MAJOR — existing users' code will break

checkpoint.explanation: The major number exists to signal exactly this. Shipping a breaking change as a patch is how version numbers stop being trustworthy. The number is a compatibility promise — that is why this is a MAJOR bump.

checkpoint.prompt: A customer reports a bug in v2.3.0, which shipped six weeks ago. What do you do first?

choices.B: Reproduce it on main first, which is close enough to the release tag
choices.C: Search the log for likely commits
choices.D: git switch --detach v2.3.0 and reproduce it on exactly that code

checkpoint.explanation: The tag lets you stand on precisely what they are running. Debugging against main means debugging code the customer does not have.
